entry: Polytheistic belief system of the Celtic peoples of Europe, also called Celtic polytheism or Celtic paganism. The Celts left no native written records of their beliefs, so evidence comes from archaeology, Greco-Roman accounts (some hostile and probably not well-informed) and early Christian-period literature. Local deities varied, but gods such as Lugus, Toutatis, Taranis, Cernunnos, Epona and Belenos were widely worshipped, and many deities were seen as threefold, as in the Three Mothers. Sacred springs were often linked to healing deities. The [[Druid|druids]] were the priests, though little is definitively known about them. Ceremonies took place in sacred groves and other natural shrines called *nemetons*, and votive offerings were deposited in water, wetlands, shafts and wells. Sacrificed animals were almost always livestock or working animals. Some evidence suggests human sacrifice, and [[Julius Caesar|Caesar]] claimed the Gauls burned criminals in a wicker man. In the 20th century the religion became the basis for Celtic neopaganism, whose groups range from Reconstructionists to New Age and Neo-Druidry.

Set of changing styles of building in ancient Egypt, most of whose surviving examples are religious and funerary structures. Because wood was scarce, the main materials were sun-dried mud brick and stone, chiefly limestone, with sandstone and granite used in considerable quantities. From the Old Kingdom onward stone was generally reserved for tombs and temples, while brick was used for palaces, fortresses and town walls. Monumental buildings used post-and-lintel construction, with thick sloping walls and closely spaced [[Column|columns]], and many were aligned astronomically. Although the [[Arch]] was developed in the fourth dynasty, monumental buildings did not adopt it. Column capitals were carved to resemble plants such as the [[Papyrus|papyrus]], and walls bore painted carvings. The best-known examples are the [[Pyramid|pyramids]] and the [[Sphinx]]. The Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak, built by [[Ramesses II]], has columns up to 20 meters high. Egyptian motifs later influenced architecture elsewhere, first in the Greek Orientalizing period and again in 19th-century Egyptomania.

Body of writing in the Egyptian language from the pharaonic period to the end of Roman domination. Writing appeared in the late 4th millennium BC, and the literature is the oldest corpus of Egyptian writing; with Sumerian literature, it is considered the world’s earliest. Old Kingdom works included funerary texts, letters, hymns, poems and autobiographies of administrative officials. A narrative literature emerged only in the early Middle Kingdom, reflecting a rising class of scribes and unprecedented literacy. Writing was an elite exercise, monopolized by scribes attached to government offices and the royal court. Popular tales included *The Story of Sinuhe* and *The Eloquent Peasant*, and teaching texts such as *The Instructions of Amenemhat* were often pseudonymous, attributed to famous figures. Texts survive on [[Papyrus|papyrus]], ostraca, wooden boards, monuments and coffins. The moist Nile floodplain destroyed most papyri, so much of the literature is lost.

Polytheistic belief system of ancient Egypt, centred on interactions with about 1,500 known deities. Rituals such as prayer and offerings sought the gods’ favor. Formal religion centred on the [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]], regarded as divine, who maintained *Ma’at*, the cosmic order, and repelled *Isfet*, chaos, through rituals and offerings. The state devoted enormous resources to temples. Individuals sought help through prayer or magic, and this popular tradition grew more prominent as the pharaoh’s status declined. Great effort went into securing the soul’s survival after death through tombs, grave goods and offerings. The religion lasted for 3,500 years. Gods rose and declined in prominence; the sun god [[Ra]], the creator god [[Amun]] and the mother goddess [[Isis]] were each at times preeminent. Under [[Akhenaten]] a single god, the Aten, briefly replaced the pantheon. After the Roman conquest in 30 BC the religion decentralized, and it was considered to have fully died in the 530s. Egyptians began converting to [[Islam]] after the Arab conquest under [[Amr ibn al-As]].

Forms of the Greek language used in ancient Greece and the ancient world from about 1500 to 300 BC. It is often divided into Mycenaean Greek (c. 1400–c. 1200 BC), the Dark Ages (c. 1200–c. 800 BC), the Archaic or Homeric period (c. 800–c. 500 BC) and the Classical period (c. 500–c. 300 BC). It was the language of [[Homer]] and of fifth- and fourth-century Athenian historians, playwrights and philosophers, and it has contributed many words to English. Its main dialect groups were Attic and Ionic, Aeolic, Arcadocypriot and Doric. Attic became the basis of Koine Greek, which followed from the [[Hellenistic period|Hellenistic period]] (c. 300 BC) and is treated as a separate stage.

Architecture of the Greek peoples from about 900 BC to the 1st century AD. It is best known for its temples, the prime example being the [[Parthenon]] in [[Athens]]. Most remains are ruins, but a number of temples survive substantially intact. The other common surviving type is the [[Theatre|open-air theatre]], the earliest dating from about 525–480 BC. Other forms include the propylon, agora, stoa, bouleuterion, mausoleum and stadium. Temples were often set on high ground and conceived as sculptural entities to be seen from all angles. Its three orders, Doric, Ionic and Corinthian, profoundly influenced later Western architecture, and Roman architecture grew out of it. Greece had abundant limestone and fine-grained white [[Marble|marble]] from Paros and Naxos, which contributed to the precision of its detail. Revivals of Classicism from the [[Renaissance]] onward kept its forms and its ideal of balance and proportion alive.

Visual and applied arts, and architecture, of the Greek peoples from the [[Iron Age]] to the Hellenistic period. Greek art is known for naturalistic but idealized depictions of the human body, with largely nude male figures the focus of innovation. Development between about 750 and 300 BC was remarkable by ancient standards and is best seen in sculpture. Painting, fine metal vessels and objects in wood are almost entirely lost. Over 100,000 significantly complete painted vessels survive, along with pottery, coins, stone sculpture and a few large bronzes. The art is usually divided into Geometric (from about 1000 BC), Archaic (including the black-figure style of the 7th century BC), Classical (from about 500 BC) and Hellenistic, which ended with the reign of [[Alexander the Great]] (336–323 BC). The transitions were gradual and local traditions varied. After [[Buddhism]] carried Greek art beyond the Greek world, it influenced Eurasian art.

Writings in the Ancient Greek language, from the earliest texts until the Byzantine period. The *Iliad* and *Odyssey* attributed to [[Homer]] are the earliest surviving works and, with the *Homeric Hymns* and the *Theogony* and *Works and Days* of [[Hesiod]], formed the foundations of the Greek literary tradition. The lyric poets [[Sappho]], Alcaeus and Pindar were highly influential. Aeschylus is the earliest tragic playwright whose complete plays survive, and [[Sophocles]] wrote *Oedipus the King* and *Antigone*. Aristophanes wrote Old Comedy. Herodotus and Thucydides, both of the fifth century BC, wrote histories of events in or near their own lifetimes. [[Plato]] wrote dialogues centred on his teacher [[Socrates]], and his student Aristotle wrote treatises that became highly influential. Later writers included Apollonius of Rhodes, author of *Argonautica*, and Plutarch. European writers since the Renaissance, including William Shakespeare, John Milton and James Joyce, drew heavily on classical themes.

Rational inquiry into the cosmos, knowledge and ethics, from the 6th century BC into the Hellenistic period. It dealt with astronomy, epistemology, mathematics, political philosophy, ethics, metaphysics, logic, biology, rhetoric and aesthetics. Philosophers before Socrates, called pre-Socratics, were concerned mainly with cosmology, ontology and mathematics, although the term is now often replaced by “Early Greek Philosophy.” [[Socrates]], [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] formed the Athenian school. Plato’s dialogues centred on Socrates, and Aristotle’s treatises integrated logic, physics, biology, ethics and politics. In the Hellenistic period, philosophy turned to personal ethics, with [[Stoicism]], Epicureanism and Skepticism as leading schools. Greek philosophy shaped Roman, early Islamic, medieval and Renaissance thought. [[Alfred North Whitehead]] described European philosophy as a series of footnotes to Plato.

Polytheistic beliefs, rituals and myths of the ancient Greeks, in both public religion and cult practice. The Greeks had no word for religion in the modern sense, and no writer classified gods or cults into separate religions; [[Herodotus]] described the Hellenes as sharing common shrines and sacrifices. Most recognized twelve major Olympian gods, including [[Zeus]], Hera, [[Poseidon]], [[Athena]] and [[Aphrodite]], although [[Stoicism]] and some forms of Platonism assumed a single transcendent deity. Zeus, king of the gods, controlled the others but was not almighty. Gods were visualized in human form and bound by fate, the *Moirai*. Cults were tied to particular cities: Athena to [[Athens]], Apollo to Delphi and Delos, and Zeus to Olympia. Greek religion extended to Ionia, [[Sicily]] and southern Italy and to colonies such as Massalia. It influenced Etruscan religion, which in turn shaped Roman religion.

Two Israelite kingdoms of the Southern Levant during the Iron Age. The Kingdom of Israel in the north and the Kingdom of Judah in the south emerged in Iron Age II, covering much of [[Canaan]]. The earliest documented mention of Israel as a people is on the Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian inscription dating to about 1208 BCE. The [[Hebrew Bible]] describes a United Monarchy under Saul, [[David]] and [[Solomon]], whose historicity is debated; historians agree that Israel and Judah existed as separate kingdoms by about 900 BCE and 850 BCE. The northern kingdom was conquered by the [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]] around 720 BCE. After Jewish revolts against Babylon, [[Nebuchadnezzar II]] destroyed Judah in 586 BCE, along with Solomon’s Temple, and exiled many Jews. After the [[Achaemenid Empire]] took Babylon around 538 BCE, [[Cyrus the Great]] issued the Edict of Cyrus, encouraging exiled Jews to return to Judah. The Second Temple was then built, beginning the Second Temple period.

Religious beliefs and practices of the civilizations of Sumer, Akkad, Assyria and Babylonia, from about 6000 BC to 500 AD. It was a consistent tradition that adapted to the needs of its adherents over millennia. Worship of natural forces as providers of sustenance is evident from the mid-4th millennium BC, when writing was invented. The [[Sumer|Sumerians]] created the first city-states, such as [[Uruk]] and [[Ur]], and developed writing, early mathematics, wheeled chariots, astronomy, a written code of law and the calendar. In the 3rd millennium BC, objects of worship became an expansive cast of deities. Later, the gods were structured into a hierarchy with the national god of each state at its head. [[Enlil]] and [[Inanna]] were among the most important figures. Worship centred on temples, daily offerings and festivals, and [[Divination|divination]] sought divine intentions. Under [[Sargon of Akkad]], the Akkadian Empire united Mesopotamia around 2335 BC. The religion declined with Christianization between the 1st and 5th centuries AD.

Athletic competitions among [[City-state|city-states]], held every four years at Olympia in honor of [[Zeus]]. Traditionally dated to 776 BC, they were one of the Panhellenic Games of ancient Greece. Each four-year period, or Olympiad, became a unit of chronology named after the winner of the stadion sprint. There were fewer events than in the [[Olympic Games|modern games]], and for many years only freeborn Greek men could compete. An Olympic truce, *ekecheiría*, let athletes and pilgrims travel safely, and victors received olive-leaf wreaths. City-states used the games to assert dominance and announce alliances. The statue of Zeus at Olympia was counted among the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]]. The last recorded celebration was in AD 393, under [[Theodosius I]]. The games probably ended under Theodosius II, possibly in connection with a fire that burned the temple of Olympian Zeus.

Architecture of ancient Rome, from the founding of the Republic in 509 BC to about the 4th century AD. It adopted the external language of classical [[Ancient Greek architecture|Greek architecture]] but developed a new style, and the two are often considered one body of classical architecture. Most surviving buildings date from the Empire, and the greatest achievements came from about 40 BC to 230 AD. Romans used [[Dome|domes]], [[Arch|arches]] and Roman concrete, moving from column-and-lintel construction to massive walls punctuated by arches. The classical orders became largely decorative, and the Tuscan and Composite orders were developed. Engineering included public and private baths, latrines, under-floor hypocaust heating, and piped water at [[Pompeii]] and Ostia. The [[Colosseum]] and the Pantheon, with its concrete dome, are among the best-known survivals. Western European building from about 1000 is called [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque]], reflecting its dependence on Roman forms.

Mystery novel by [[Agatha Christie]], first published in 1939. It is the world’s best-selling mystery novel, with more than 100 million copies sold by 2007. Ten people accused of past crimes are killed one by one on an isolated island off the [[Devon]] coast, following a popular rhyme. Christie considered it the most difficult of her novels to write. The first British edition used a racially offensive title, which was later changed; the American edition has used its current title since 1940.

Southernmost autonomous community of [[Spain]] (pop., 2025: 8,676,713). It is the most populous and second-largest autonomous community in Spain, with eight provinces: Almería, Cádiz, Córdoba, Granada, Huelva, Jaén, Málaga and Seville. Its capital is [[Seville]]. The name derives from [[Al-Andalus]], first attested on dinars minted in 716 by the new Muslim government of Iberia. During the Islamic Golden Age, Córdoba surpassed Constantinople to become Europe’s biggest city. The Crown of Castile conquered the Guadalquivir Valley in the 13th century, and the Emirate of [[Granada]] was subdued in the late 15th century. Agriculture remains vital, and mass tourism has been a staple since the 1960s. Many internationally recognized Spanish cultural forms are distinctively Andalusian in origin, including [[Flamenco|flamenco]]. The hinterland is the hottest area of Europe, with Córdoba and Seville averaging above 36 °C (97 °F) in summer highs.

Spanish riding horse breed, also called the *Pura Raza Española* (PRE) or Pure Spanish Horse, from the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. Its ancestors have lived there for thousands of years, and it has been recognized as a distinct breed since the 15th century, its conformation changing little. Prized as a war horse by the nobility, it served as a tool of Spanish diplomacy, and kings across Europe owned Spanish horses. Warfare, disease and crossbreeding reduced herds in the 19th century, and exports were restricted until the 1960s. More than 185,000 registered Andalusians existed worldwide in 2010. The breed is strongly built and elegant, with long, thick manes and tails, and most are gray. Known for intelligence and docility, it was originally used for classical dressage, driving, [[Bullfighting|bullfighting]] and working livestock. It is closely related to the Lusitano and has contributed to many European warmbloods and to the Azteca.

Marginal sea of the northeastern Indian Ocean, historically also called the Burma Sea. It is bounded by [[Myanmar]] and [[Thailand]] along the Gulf of Martaban and the west side of the Malay Peninsula, and is separated from the [[Bay of Bengal]] by the [[Andaman and Nicobar Islands]]. Its southern exit is the [[Strait of Malacca]], 3 km wide and 37 m deep. The northern and eastern parts are shallow, with the continental shelf extending over 200 km off Myanmar and Thailand, while the western and central areas are 900–3,000 m deep. Silt from the [[Irrawaddy River]] shallows the north. The sea supports fisheries, shipping and coral-reef tourism. The December 2004 [[2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami|Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami]] severely damaged its fishing and tourist infrastructure.

Union territory of India (pop., 2011: 380,581) comprising 836 islands, of which only 31 are inhabited. The islands form two clusters, the northern Andaman Islands and the southern Nicobar Islands, separated by the 150 km-wide Ten Degree Channel. The capital, Port Blair, lies about 1,190 km (740 mi) from [[Chennai]]. The indigenous Andamanese may have been isolated from other populations for more than 30,000 years. The Danish were the first Europeans to arrive, in 1755. The islands became part of the [[British Raj]] in 1868 and were invaded by the [[Empire of Japan]] during [[World War II]]. They became a union territory under the Constitution of India in 1950. They host the Andaman and Nicobar Command, the only geographical command jointly run by India’s Army, Air Force and Navy. [[North Sentinel Island]] is home to the Sentinelese, an uncontacted tribe.

New World vulture of the [[Andes]], generally considered the largest [[Bird of prey|bird of prey]]. Its maximum wingspan is 3.3 m (10 ft 10 in), and it has a weight of 15 kg (33 lb). Males have a fleshy comb and large white wing patches, while females are smaller, unusually among birds of prey. A scavenger, it prefers large carcasses such as those of deer or cattle, and it can live more than 70 years in some cases. It is a national symbol of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. The IUCN lists it as vulnerable, threatened by habitat loss and by lead poisoning from carcasses killed by hunters.

Norwegian mass murderer and domestic terrorist. He detonated a car bomb in Oslo’s government quarter and then shot people at a Labour Party youth camp on Utøya island, in the [[2011 Norway attacks]], killing 77 people and injuring over 323. He had earlier chaired the Vest Oslo youth branch of the anti-immigration Progress Party. His manifesto opposed Islam and blamed feminism for a perceived European “cultural suicide.” Convicted in 2012, he received 21 years of preventive detention, extendable while he is judged a danger to society. Psychiatric evaluations disagreed: one diagnosed paranoid schizophrenia, while another found narcissistic and antisocial personality disorder.

American broadcast journalist and political commentator. He anchors the [[CNN]] program *Anderson Cooper 360°*, and for two decades he was a correspondent for CBS News’s *60 Minutes*. After graduating from [[Yale University]] in 1989, he reported from war-torn regions and joined ABC News in 1995. His coverage of [[Hurricane Katrina]] greatly increased his popularity, and he received Haiti’s National Order of Honour and Merit for his coverage of the 2010 Haiti earthquake. He has won 18 Emmy Awards and two Peabody Awards. A member of the [[Vanderbilt family]], he came out as gay in 2012.

State on the east coast of southern India, the seventh largest in India by area. Telugu, one of India’s classical languages, is the official and most widely spoken language. Amaravati is the capital and [[Visakhapatnam]] the largest city. The [[Satavahana dynasty]] ruled most of the Deccan from the 1st to 3rd century CE, and later rulers included the [[Vijayanagara Empire]]. The British controlled much of the area as part of the Madras Presidency for two centuries. Andhra State was formed in 1953 and merged with the Telugu-speaking regions of Hyderabad State in 1956 to form Andhra Pradesh. [[Telangana]] was separated from it in 2014. Agriculture employed 62.2% of the population as of September 2020, with [[Rice|rice]] the staple crop. The state produced 30% of India’s fish in 2022–23, and the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota is India’s primary satellite launch centre.

Landlocked microstate in the eastern Pyrenees, between [[France]] and [[Spain]] (pop., July 2026: 90,021). Believed to have been created by [[Charlemagne]], it was ruled by the count of Urgell until 988, when it passed to the Diocese of Urgell. It was formed as a polity by a charter in 1278 and was a lordship within the Principality of [[Catalonia]] until 1715. It is headed by two co-princes, the Bishop of Urgell and the president of France. Its capital, Andorra la Vella, is the highest capital city in Europe, at 1,023 m. The sole official language is Catalan. Tourism brings about 8 million visitors a year. Andorra is not a member of the [[European Union]], but it has belonged to the [[United Nations]] and the [[Council of Europe]] since 1993, and it adopted the [[Euro|euro]] in 2002.

French physicist and mathematician, one of the founders of classical electromagnetism. He referred to the field as electrodynamics and made contributions to chemistry and philosophy. Largely self-taught, he became a professor at the École polytechnique and the Collège de France and was a member of the French Academy of Sciences. He coined the term *solenoid* and invented the electrical telegraph. His work on the forces between current-carrying wires followed Hans Christian Ørsted’s discovery of electromagnetism in 1820. His name is one of 72 inscribed on the [[Eiffel Tower]]. The SI unit of [[Electric current|electric current]], the [[Ampere|ampere]], is named after him.
